sourceEdition: 2021 Illustrative Mathematics K–5 source teacher lesson and Student Facing
sourceActivity1: Students draw one-third then one-quarter of that third AND one-quarter then one-third of that quarter as two diagrams; each shaded area is 1/12 of the original whole.
sourceActivity2: Original Kendall Hunt IM2021 public teacher Student Facing Activity 2 has two distinct unit squares: image record 149035 contains two equal rows and five equal columns, one shaded (1/10); separate image record 149036 has five equal rows and three equal columns, one shaded (1/15). Explain 1/5×1/2 and 1/2×1/5 for first, and 1/3×1/5 and 1/5×1/3 for second, relative to each original whole. Drawings, justifications and source figure interpretation are teacher-scored; diagrams included in Edulytiks are first-party alternatives.
studentFacingFormativeTask: Draw two equal-size full-unit squares. Shade one fourth of one third in the first and one third of one fourth in the second. Compare their shaded areas and explain why both are 1/12 of the ORIGINAL whole. Then explain a separate 1/5×1/2 square and write both 1/5×1/2 and 1/2×1/5 for the same one-tenth area. Compare the distinct original five-row, three-column Student Facing image with Priya's two-row, five-column image. Explain why the second image represents 1/15, not 1/10, and write both multiplication orders.

rubric.criterion: Both complete equal-size original unit squares are shown and explicitly identified as wholes
First square is partitioned into three equal thirds and one chosen third into four equal parts; full-square equal-area coverage
Second square partitions into four equal quarters and one selected quarter into three equal parts; full-square equal-area coverage
One marked cell of twelve, same absolute area in both orders; 1/12 of original whole justified
Priya example explains both 1/5×1/2 and 1/2×1/5 as 1/10 of the same whole, not 1/5 or 1/2 of whole
Separate original source diagram 149036 is a 5-row-by-3-column equal-area unit square with one shaded cell; 1/15 is justified visually by 1/5×1/3 or 1/3×1/5, without confusing this with Priya's 1/10.
